title: Stratford-upon-Avon
subtitle: Shakespeare the businessman
intro: Sunday afternoon in Stratford-upon-Avon. Everyone knows Shakespeare as a poet. This is the other story: a family that lost its place, a man who made money and won it back, and a grave with a curse on it.

acts.label: Act 1 · Born on the slide
acts.tagline: The family that lost its place.
acts.narrative: His father made gloves, rose to the top job in the town, then lost his money. The first record of the family is a fine for a muck heap in this street.

acts.label: Act 2 · The free school
acts.narrative: A free school paid for by the town. He never went to university, which is why some people still say someone else wrote his plays.

acts.label: Act 3 · The businessman
acts.tagline: Rich from owning, not from writing.
acts.narrative: He made his money from owning a share of a theatre company. He bought one of the biggest houses in town, and got his father a coat of arms.

acts.label: Act 4 · The grave, and what he left
acts.tagline: A grave he paid for. Words we still use.
acts.narrative: He bought the right to be buried by the altar. His friends saved his plays. And his words are still in the way we talk.

planNote.text: Book the Birthplace online before you leave: it has timed entry, and the same ticket gets you into New Place (£25 online, £27 at the door). Pick a slot about 3:30. New Place: last entry 2:30. Holy Trinity closes at 3:15 on Sundays. Waterside is closed to cars until 6 PM for a market, so don't drive that way. Weather (Met Office, this morning): cloudy at 2, light showers 3–4 PM (60%), sunny spells again about 5. Sunset 6:06.

planArrival.title: Done by about 5:45
planArrival.note: Walk back to Bridgeway car park, about 5 minutes. Pay at the machine on the way out. Sunset is 6:06.

park.name: Park and walk to New Place
park.angle: Park, then straight to New Place
park.story: Park at Bridgeway multi-storey car park, by Clopton Bridge (CV37 6YX). The first hour is free, and 4 hours is £5.80. Card only: it reads your number plate, and you pay at the machine before you leave. Height limit 1.8 m. Running late? Church Street car park (CV37 6HB) is 3 minutes from New Place.

routeCard.sub: Bridgeway car park · CV37 6YX · arrive about 2:00 PM
routeCard.note: Card only. You pay on the way out, so you can't overstay.

see: Harvard House on High Street (1596). It was the family home of John Harvard's mother. Harvard University is named after him.
planCard.todo: Walk straight to New Place, about 9 minutes. Last entry is 2:30.

new-place.name: Shakespeare's New Place
new-place.story: Last entry is 2:30, so come here first. Your Birthplace ticket gets you in. The house has gone. Today it's a garden where the house stood.
new-place.onCamera: Shakespeare bought a house here when he was 33. He died in it.
facts: He didn't get rich from writing. He got rich because he owned a share of his acting company, and a share of the Globe Theatre in London.
In 1597 he bought this house, one of the biggest in town. The year before, he got his father a coat of arms. The motto was 'Not without right.' The glove-maker's family were gentlemen now.
new-place.closeOnCamera: So where's the house? In the 1750s a vicar called Francis Gastrell owned it. Tourists kept coming, so he cut down Shakespeare's mulberry tree. Then he had a row with the town about tax, and in 1759 he knocked the whole house down. The town was so angry that he had to leave.

routeCard.note: Enter from Chapel Street. Your Birthplace ticket gets you in.

see: The garden where Shakespeare's house stood
planCard.todo: Then walk down Church Street to the church, about 8 minutes.

church-street.name: The Guild Chapel and his school
church-street.story: On the walk from New Place to the church. The chapel is open until 4, and free. The schoolroom is upstairs in the old Guildhall, next to it. Don't stop long: the church closes at 3:15.
church-street.onCamera: This is almost certainly where Shakespeare went to school.
facts: It was a free school for boys from the town. Lessons were in Latin, from early morning to late afternoon, Monday to Saturday.
Nobody can prove he came here. But it was free, it was five minutes from his house, and his father had been bailiff.
church-street.closeOnCamera: And here's the thing. He never went to university. That's why some people still say a nobleman must have written his plays. Almost every historian disagrees.

routeCard.sub: Church Street · on the way to the church

see: The old Guildhall and the schoolroom
The timber almshouses next door, from the 1400s
planCard.todo: Keep walking. The church closes at 3:15.

holy-trinity.name: Holy Trinity Church
holy-trinity.story: Open today only until 3:15. Walk up the avenue of lime trees to the door. The grave costs £5 to see. It's a working church, so keep your voice down.
holy-trinity.onCamera: Shakespeare is buried in this church. And he paid for the spot.
facts: Most people were buried outside, in the churchyard. In 1605 he paid £440 for a share of the church's income. That gave him the right to be buried in here, next to the altar.

Seven years after he died, two actors from his company printed his plays in one big book, the First Folio. Eighteen of the plays had never been printed before, including Macbeth and The Tempest. Without that book, we would probably have lost them.
holy-trinity.closeOnCamera: Now read his gravestone: 'Cursed be he that moves my bones.' In 2016, scientists scanned the grave with radar. The head end looks disturbed. That fits an old story that someone stole his skull. The church isn't convinced.

routeCard.note: Go in by the avenue of lime trees.

planCard.todo: Pay £5 for the grave. Be out by 3:15. Then walk up to Henley Street, about 13 minutes.

birthplace.name: Shakespeare's Birthplace
birthplace.angle: Born into a family on the slide
birthplace.story: Timed entry: use the slot you booked. Last entry is 4:30. It's indoors, which is good: showers are forecast from 3 to 4.
birthplace.onCamera: This is the house where Shakespeare was born, in 1564.
facts: The first record of his family is right here. In April 1552, his father was fined 12 pence for a muck heap in this street.

His father made gloves. He rose to bailiff, the top job in the town. Then his business failed, he got into debt, and his application for a coat of arms went nowhere. William grew up watching his family lose its place.
birthplace.closeOnCamera: And I think that explains him. The money, the big house, the coat of arms he got later: it was all about winning that place back.

routeCard.note: Enter through the Shakespeare Centre on Henley Street. Timed entry.

see: The room where he was born
The old timber fronts of Henley Street
planCard.todo: Stay inside through the showers. Then walk down to the river, about 7 minutes.

river.name: The river: the statue, the theatre and the bridge
river.story: Bancroft Gardens, by the canal basin. The statue is Shakespeare, with four of his characters around him: Hamlet, Lady Macbeth, Falstaff and Prince Hal. Clopton Bridge was built around 1484 by Hugh Clopton, the same man who built New Place. There's a market along Waterside until 6, so it will be busy.
river.onCamera: Shakespeare died 400 years ago. You still use his words every day.
facts: 'Green-eyed monster.' 'The be-all and end-all.' 'It's all Greek to me.' They all come from his plays. People say he invented 1,700 words. That's an exaggeration, but hundreds of words and phrases reached us through him.

He also shaped how England sees its own past. He made Richard the Third a villain, writing under Queen Elizabeth, whose grandfather took Richard's crown. And in 1944 the government paid for a film of Henry the Fifth, to lift spirits around D-Day.
river.closeOnCamera: And this theatre opened on 23 April 1932, the day Stratford celebrates his birthday. It was designed by Elisabeth Scott. She was 29, and the only woman out of 70 architects in the competition. A glove-maker's son from a market town. And 400 years later: a theatre, a statue, and the words we speak.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
facts: The hook: 'Everyone knows this man as a poet. But there's another story about him that I'd like to tell you.'
What this is: one afternoon in Stratford-upon-Avon, where Shakespeare was born, got rich, and is buried.
The promise: a family that lost its place, a man who won it back, and a grave with a curse on it.

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: Where you are: by the river, under his statue.
The recap: born into a family on the slide, rich from owning a theatre, buried in a grave he paid for, and still in the words we use.
The ask: like and subscribe, and tell me where I should go next.
